In your letter, you also alleged that the Mayor entered into the said contract without obtaining any authority from the Sa-tgguniang Bayan of Midsayap. •In repiy, we limit the issues to whether a local chief executive as Head of the Procuring Entity can terminate a procurement contract prior to its implementation; if in the affirmative, whether an Executive Order is a valid act to effect a termination of a procuremenv contract; and, finally, in the event of •a review which invalidates an Executive Order annulling a contract, what is the status of the contract? Discussion On the Fin f (ssue: The Local Chief' Executive as Head of the Procuring Entity can terminate urement contract. A nief executive is vested with powers upon which one can exercise and perform the Guties under Republic Act No. 7160 or the Local Government Code of 1991 ('LG Code').

This is consistent to the exercise of one of the corporate powers of a local government unit under Section 224 of the LG Code. As e contracting party and representative of the municipality, a municipal mayor is bound to respect the provisions of the contract which likewise includes provision for termination. Che binding effeet of any agreement between the parties to a contract is premised settled principles: (l) that obligations arising from contracts have the force of between the contracting parties; and (2) that there must be mutuality between tie parties based on their essential equality to which is repugnant to have one party boun,i hy Lhe contract leaving the other free therefrom.5 Thus, in the exercise of the powers granted upon him under the LG Code, a local chief executive, or in this case, a municipal mayor, may terminate an existing contract. It is deemed a valid exercise of such powers. On the Secom! Issue: The determination whether an Evecutive Order may be one of the means to the termination ofa procurement contract, is a justiciable issue which only the pueo.•r court can determine. On issue of whether an EO by itself is a valid act to cause the termination or nullificatie•i of the procurement contract, it is our view that the same should be adjudicated i: lhe proper courts because the facts are in the nature of justiciable issues. We also take note that the governing guidelines under the procurement law does prescribe the manner or form of the order which shall be the final document completing the termination after complying with the procedures given. With more reason that the Department is ill no position to determine the same. Pursuant to DILG Memorandum Order No. , this Department is constrained from rendering an opinion where another government agency, such as the GPPB, exercises primary authority or expertise on the subject matter of the query, that is, the termination of a procuremen• ccntract. On the Third Issue: IVichout ruling on the validity of EO No. 40 which cancelled, terminated, and nullified the procurement contract, the status of said contract remains as such In the review of the subject EO conducted by the Governor of Cotabato who invalidated EO No. 40, it is our view that the same should be confined to the determinatie»• whether an executive order is consistent with the laws in order to rule on its validity, as stated in Section of RA 7160 or the Local (rvernment Code of 1991 (LG Code) In all instances of the review, the local chief executive shall ensure that such executive are within the powers granted by law and in conformity with provincial, city, or mtnucipal ordinances.7 Administrative or executive acts, orders and regulations shall be only when they are not contrary to the laws or the Constitution.8 In this case, the Governor of Cotabato found invalid EO No. 40 for several reasons. Based on the review, the main basis for promulgating EO No. 40 was the findings of the Ad Hoe Committee which was created pursuant to EO No. 26, Series of 2013, an order which did noc pass the review of the Provincial Governor of Cotabato. On this premise, the committee findings and recommendations were rendered of doubtful legality and validity, including the basis for zhe issuance of EO No. 40. Further, the review went to the extent ef upholding the validity of the procurement contract on the provision of Build and t iamsfer scheme, contrary to the legal premises cited in EO No. 40. These acts of the reviewing authority appear to be beyond what is required under Section 30 (a) and (b) of RA 7!60. The •eninent issue henceforth touches on the status of the contract after the Governor o? held invalid EO No. 40. EO No. 40, which you promulgated, terminated the procurement contract. This Department will not intervene to rule on its procedural and substantive validity because to do so is to arrogate the powers of the judiciary in the determination of a justiciable issue. We were asked to determine the status of contract after you terminated it. The Department has no further role determine its status - the contract remains as such, upon exercising the powers granted to local chief executives under the LG Code. Under Section 22(c) of RA 7160, the local chief executive cannot enter into a contract in behalf of the local government unit (LGU) without prior authorization from the sanggunian concerned. 9 To reconcile this provision relative to procurement under RA 9184, the case of Quisumbing vs Garcia10 explains this further by indicating the circumstances when a prior authorization from the local sanggunian is required or not: "R.A. No. 9184 establishes the lavv and procedure for public Sec. 317 thereof' explicitly makes the approval of the ap, ,rpriate authority which, in the case of local government units, is the sang»unian, the point Offreference for the notice to proceed to be issued to the 'Winning bidder. This provision, rather than being in conflict with or providing an exception to Sec. 22(c) of' R.A. No. 7160, blends seamlessly with the latter and even acknowledges that in the exercise of the local government unit's corporate powers, the chief executive acts merely as an instrumentality of the local council. Read together, the cited provisions mandate the local chief executive to secure the san nian's approval before entering into pncurement contracts and to tral •mit the notice to proceed to the winning bidder not later than seven (7) calendar days therefrom. The question of "'hether a sanggunian authorization separate from •the gppropriation ordinance is required should he resolved depending on the :vrricular circumslances of the case. Resort to the appropriation is necessary m order to determine if there is a provision therein which specifically cove,'3 the expense to be incurred or the contract to be entered into. Should Ehe appropriation ordinance, for instance, already contain in sufficient detail the project and cost ofa capital outlay such [hat all that the local chief executive needs to do after undergoing the requisite public bidding is to execute the contract, no further authorization is required, the appropriation ordinance already being sufficient. the other hand. should the appropriation ordinance describe the proje,.u:: in generic terms such as "infrastructure projects, " "inter-municipal waterworks, drainage and sewerage, flood control, and irrigation systems prouec:s, " "reclamation projects " or "roads and bridges, " there is an obvious need for a covering contract for every specific project that in turn requires approval by the sanggunien.
